story.title: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1

facts.text: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.
Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits.
But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems.
Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.
Google under Alphabet Inc. (GOOG) is preparing to launch its first experimental satellite as part of Project Suncatcher, an ambitious effort to develop AI data centers in orbit.
The spacecraft was built by Planet Labs, allowing Google to accelerate its testing rather than develop a satellite from scratch.
Google plans additional launches in 2027 but expects Suncatcher will remain years away from becoming a commercial product.

Google is set to launch its first experimental satellite for “Project Suncatcher” on October 1, marking a significant step toward its goal of building orbital AI data centres powered by near-constant sunlight.
Experts caution the concept remains years from commercial viability due to high launch costs and engineering constraints.
Google stressed the first mission is about gathering data and recognising and identifying failure points, not showcasing an operational orbital data centre.
The satellite will run Gemini models for testing.
Future designs envision clusters of satellites carrying dozens of TPUs each, communicating via high-bandwidth lasers.
Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test those laser links.
The refrigerator-sized satellite, named MVP, will carry four of Google’s custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
The spacecraft was built in partnership with satellite imagery firm Planet Labs.
The mission will assess how Google’s TPUs withstand launch forces, radiation, and thermal extremes.
Google said its Trillium TPUs held up well in ground tests, surviving radiation doses greater than what a five-year space mission would deliver.
In space, there’s no airflow; heat must be diffused via radiators.
Google’s design combines heat pipes and radiators, but the system can only run in roughly 15-minute bursts before the TPUs must shut down to let radiators catch up.
Google will launch its first experimental satellite for Project Suncatcher on October 1.
The mission will test whether space can support future AI data centres powered by near-constant sunlight.
The satellite will run Gemini models during the test mission.
Future plans include clusters carrying dozens of TPUs and communicating through high-bandwidth laser links.
Google plans to launch two additional satellites in 2027 to test those connections.
However, experts say commercial orbital data centres remain years away because of launch costs and technical challenges.

The refrigerator-sized satellite, named MVP, will carry four Google Tensor Processing Units.
Google developed the spacecraft with satellite imagery company Planet Labs.
Cooling remains one of the project’s major engineering challenges.
Space lacks airflow, so the satellite must release heat through radiators.
Google’s design uses heat pipes and radiators, but the TPUs can operate for only about 15 minutes before cooling becomes necessary.
